title: Cache Locality and Data-Oriented Design
objectives: Compute the padding, sizeof and cache-line utilisation of a given struct layout
Explain why sequential, contiguous access out-performs pointer-chasing at hardware level
Convert an array-of-structs design into a struct-of-arrays layout for a stated hot loop
Identify false sharing and describe how to avoid it in multi-threaded tick handlers
motivation: A feed handler must scan one million quotes and recompute spreads on every tick. The arithmetic is trivial, one subtraction per quote, yet a naive object-oriented layout can run this loop three to five times slower than a hardware-friendly one, purely because of where the bytes sit. At 200+ cycles per DRAM access, memory locality, not FLOPs, decides who gets the fill.

blocks.text: The machine you are really programming

blocks.md: At 3 GHz the CPU retires one instruction roughly every 0.33 ns, but register-adjacent data is only the beginning of the story. Hitting **L1** cache costs about 4 cycles, **L2** about 12, **L3** about 40, and **DRAM** 200 or more. A single main-memory stall is therefore longer than 600 instructions of actual work. The cache moves data in fixed **cache lines**, typically 64 bytes, so touching even 1 byte drags the whole line in. Two consequences dominate performance engineering: *temporal locality* (reuse data soon after touching it) and *spatial locality* (touch neighbouring bytes together, because the hardware already fetched them).

blocks.caption: One 64-byte cache line. Hardware prefetchers fetch these in sequence, contiguity is what lets the CPU hide DRAM latency entirely.

blocks.title: Latency in trading terms
blocks.md: If your tick-to-trade path takes 2 microseconds and you add 10 cache misses at ~70 ns each (L3/DRAM mix), you have just burned 0.7 microseconds, over a third of your budget, without writing any new logic. Layout is a latency decision.

blocks.text: Array of structs vs struct of arrays

blocks.md: Object-oriented habit says: one `Quote` object holding everything a quote *is*. Hardware says: one array of the fields the hot loop *uses*. The first is **AoS** (array of structs), the second **SoA** (struct of arrays). Consider a market-data hot loop that only reads `bid` and `ask`:

blocks.caption: sizeof says 24, but the cache-line arithmetic is what predicts speed.
SoA: the fields the loop ignores are physically absent from its cache traffic.

blocks.md: The cost model is blunt. For $n = 10^6$ quotes, the AoS spread loop streams $24 \times 10^6$ bytes of cache lines while using only $16 \times 10^6$ - a third of memory bandwidth wasted. SoA streams exactly $16 \times 10^6$ useful bytes. Worse, AoS *mixes* cold fields (`symId`, `stale`) into the same lines as hot fields, so the cache fills with bytes the loop never reads.

blocks.text: Data-oriented design: organise for the access pattern

blocks.md: **Data-oriented design (DOD)** inverts the usual process: start from the hot loops, list what they touch per iteration, then choose the layout that minimises bytes moved. Practical rules: keep hot arrays contiguous and index-based (no pointer chasing, each hop is a potential cache miss the prefetcher cannot predict); split hot from cold fields; store fixed-size records so indexing is $\text{base} + i \times \text{size}$ arithmetic; batch work so each cache line fetched is fully consumed. Virtual functions and per-object heap allocation fight DOD because they hide where the bytes actually are.

One multi-threaded trap deserves its own mention: **false sharing**. If two threads write different variables that happen to live on the *same* 64-byte line, the cache-coherence protocol shuttles the line between cores on every write, costing hundreds of cycles per access, even though the threads never share data. Fix: pad or align hot per-thread data so each thread owns whole lines.

blocks.caption: alignas(64) makes each counters element occupy its own cache line.

blocks.title: Measure, then restructure
blocks.md: SoA is not free: field-wise arrays make single-record updates touch several distant locations, and some code gets uglier. Restructure for the loops that dominate profiles (measure first, see the benchmarking lesson), not for aesthetics.

guidedExercise.prompt: Given `struct Tick { double price; long qty; char flags; };` on a 64-bit machine (8-byte alignment), compute: (a) `sizeof(Tick)` with padding; (b) how many whole `Tick` objects fit in one 64-byte cache line; (c) the fraction of a cache line that carries useful `price` bytes for a loop that only reads prices.
hints: Lay members out in declaration order, then round the total up to a multiple of the largest alignment (8).
guidedExercise.solution: (a) `price` occupies offsets 0-7, `qty` 8-15, `flags` offset 16, then 7 bytes of padding -> `sizeof = 24`. (b) $\lfloor 64/24 \rfloor = 2$ whole ticks per line (48 bytes used, 16 idle). (c) Two ticks per line contribute $2 \times 8 = 16$ useful `price` bytes, so utilisation $= 16/64 = 25\%$. An SoA layout of prices alone would be $8 \times 8 = 64$ bytes of pure prices per line - $100\%$.

independentExercise.prompt: A book scanner loops over 250,000 instruments reading only each instrument's `bestBid` and `bestAsk` (two `double`s each). Currently the instruments live in an AoS vector where each record is `bestBid`, `bestAsk`, `symbolName[16]` (16 bytes of `char`), and `std::int32_t venueId`. Compute: (a) `sizeof` the record; (b) bytes of cache traffic per scan in AoS; (c) bytes of cache traffic per scan after an SoA split that stores only the two doubles contiguously; (d) the percentage of bandwidth saved.
hints: Member sizes: 8 + 8 + 16 + 4 = 36; round up to the alignment of the largest member (8).
In SoA, the scanner streams two arrays of 8-byte doubles; traffic = 2 x 8 bytes per instrument.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $8+8+16+4 = 36$, padded to a multiple of 8 gives `sizeof = 40`. (b) AoS traffic $= 250{,}000 \times 40 = 10^7$ bytes (10 MB), of which only 16 bytes per record are useful. (c) SoA traffic $= 250{,}000 \times 16 = 4 \times 10^6$ bytes (4 MB). (d) Saving $= (10-4)/10 = 60\%$ less memory traffic, and every fetched line is now 100% useful, so the prefetcher streams perfectly.

commonMistakes: Believing big-O alone predicts speed: two O(n) loops can differ 3-5x purely on layout and cache-line utilisation.
Counting sizeof as the whole story: alignment padding inside arrays means sizeof(record) records per line, not sizeof(fields) worth of data.
Chasing pointers (linked lists, node-based containers) in hot loops, each hop can be an unpredictable cache miss.
Letting threads write distinct variables that share a cache line (false sharing) and blaming the 'slow CPU'.
realWorldApplication: Game engines, scientific codes and HFT systems all converge on SoA layouts with cache-line-aligned hot structures; the same arithmetic you did above is exactly what a feed-handler author computes before choosing the quote-store design.
quantFinanceApplication: A pricing hot loop that recomputes spreads or marks across a million instruments is bandwidth-bound: cutting per-instrument cache traffic from 40 to 16 bytes directly reduces tick-to-trade latency and lets one core handle more instruments per tick.
summary: Memory moves in 64-byte cache lines; L1 ~4 cycles vs DRAM ~200+ cycles makes locality the first-order performance factor.
AoS interleaves hot and cold bytes; SoA gives each hot loop its own contiguous, fully-used cache lines.
Compute layout impact with arithmetic: struct size, records per line, useful-bytes fraction.
False sharing is coherence traffic on lines shared by accident; fix with alignment/padding, not locks.
Data-oriented design starts from hot loops and chooses the layout that minimises bytes moved.

quiz.prompt: A 64-bit machine, 8-byte alignment. What is sizeof of `struct Quote { double bid; double ask; std::int32_t symId; bool stale; };` in bytes?
quiz.explanation: 8 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 21 bytes of members; the struct's alignment is 8 (largest member is double), so the total is rounded up to 24 with 3 trailing padding bytes.

quiz.prompt: How many 8-byte doubles fit in one 64-byte cache line?
quiz.explanation: 64 / 8 = 8 doubles per line, which is why an SoA array of doubles achieves 100% cache-line utilisation.

quiz.prompt: A spread-scan loop reads only `bid` and `ask` from the 24-byte `Quote` struct above, stored as a big AoS vector. Roughly what fraction of the cache-line bytes it fetches is useful?
options: ~50%: each 64-byte line holds 2 whole quotes (48 bytes) but only their bid+ask bytes (32) are read
~75%: 3 of 4 fields are read per quote
quiz.explanation: 24 does not divide 64: each line carries 2 whole quotes = 48 bytes (16 bytes of the line idle), and the loop reads only bid+ask = 32 bytes of those 48. Useful/total = 32/64 = 50%.

quiz.prompt: Two worker threads each increment a different `uint64_t` counter, but the counters sit 8 bytes apart in one array. Profiling shows huge time in 'coherence stalls'. What is this, and the standard fix?
options: False sharing; fix by padding/aligning so each thread's data occupies its own cache line
Cache aliasing; fix by changing the allocator
A mispredicted branch; fix by restructuring the loop
quiz.explanation: The counters are distinct, but they share one 64-byte cache line, so the coherence protocol ping-pongs the line between cores on every write. alignas(64) or padding separates them onto different lines.

quiz.prompt: Which change most directly improves spatial locality for a hot scan loop over market records?
options: Replacing contiguous arrays with a linked list of heap-allocated record objects
Splitting the record into SoA arrays so the loop's fields are contiguous and nothing cold is interleaved
Adding virtual methods to the record class for extensibility
Increasing the struct size so records are 'rounder'
quiz.explanation: SoA makes the touched fields one sequential stream, every fetched line is fully used and prefetchable. Pointer chasing kills prefetching; virtual calls obscure layout; bigger structs waste bandwidth.
sizeof is 24 (21 bytes of members padded to the 8-byte alignment), and integer division 64/24 = 2 whole quotes per 64-byte cache line.

flashcards.front: What is a cache line and why does it matter?
flashcards.back: The unit (typically 64 bytes) in which caches move data. Touching 1 byte fetches the whole line, so neighbouring bytes are nearly free and distant bytes are not.

AoS: one struct per record, all fields together, good for whole-record access. SoA: one contiguous array per field, good for hot loops touching a few fields, gives 100% cache-line utilisation and streamable prefetch.

flashcards.front: Cache-line utilisation of a hot loop
flashcards.back: useful bytes read per line / 64. E.g. reading bid+ask (16 B) from 24-byte Quotes: 2 quotes/line -> 32 useful of 64 = 50%.
Two threads writing different variables that share one cache line, causing coherence traffic between cores even though no data is logically shared. Fix: align/pad to one line per thread's data.
